title: Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet II: Enkidu comes to Uruk
source: British Museum tablet photographs + eBL manuscript transliterations (eBL corpus edition L I.4, Poem of Gilgamesh (ed. A. R. George, rev. G. Rozzi and E. Jiménez), SB II) + English of the eBL edition (A. R. George (eBL edition))
description: Standard Babylonian Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet II: 118 of 187 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (6 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and A. R. George's English translation.
introduction:
Shamhat leads Enkidu to the shepherds, where he learns to eat bread and drink ale. He goes to Uruk, blocks Gilgamesh's way, and the two wrestle and become friends. Gilgamesh proposes an expedition to the Forest of Cedar to kill its guardian Humbaba; Enkidu and the elders of Uruk warn him against it.

The Standard Babylonian version of the epic, traditionally ascribed to the scholar Sin-leqi-unninni, was written on twelve tablets. Most surviving copies come from the libraries of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh (7th century BCE) and from Babylon and other Babylonian cities (7th-2nd century BCE). This page gives Tablet II in the line numbering of the electronic Babylonian Library edition by A. R. George (2022 and later revisions).

How this page is built. Each section is a run of consecutive lines as written on one photographed clay tablet. For every line the eBL edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/4/SB/II) lists the manuscripts that carry it, with each tablet's own column and line numbers; the tablet chosen for each run is the photographed copy of the work with the most signs preserved there. Commentaries and texts that only quote a line are never chosen. School and excerpt tablets are used only for lines that no photographed library copy preserves as well, and only where they carry the line as text; their sections say so. The original text is eBL's transliteration of that tablet's signs (not a modern composite text): square brackets mark broken signs, x an illegible sign, # a damaged sign, ? an uncertain reading, and words in {braces} are determinatives; the notes give a key to every sign used on this page, and eBL's layout codes are written out in words (for example '(line break)' or '(blank space)'). Superscript numbers are the line numbers of the eBL edition, used in both the Akkadian and the English. The English is A. R. George's translation in the eBL edition (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), one line of English per line of the poem; italics mark uncertain renderings, as in the source. Where the tablet is broken, the English still translates the whole line of eBL's composite text; each section's note names the lines that are broken on its tablet.

Finding a line on the photograph. Each section names the tablet, the face and column, and the tablet's own line numbers (a prime, as in 5', counts from the first preserved line of a broken column). On a tablet with six columns the obverse carries columns i-iii from left to right; the reverse, turned over from bottom to top, carries columns iv-vi from right to left. The photographs often show the obverse above the reverse with the edges around them; a fragment preserves only part of this layout.

This page shows 118 of the 187 lines of the eBL edition (63%), from 6 tablets in the British Museum: BM.38538, Rm.289 (Nineveh), K.8574 (Nineveh), BM.38833, BM.34449, BM.40849.

Lines not shown. 69 of the 187 lines of the eBL edition are not shown, because no photographed copy of the work used here carries them: 26-36 (no photograph in eBL: IM.76941 (Iraq Museum)); 37-41 (no photograph in eBL: ISACM-A.3444 (Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, Chicago), IM.76941 (Iraq Museum)); 56-58 (photograph does not show these lines (visual check): BM.34964); a+1'-a+4' (no photograph in eBL: ISACM-A.3444 (Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, Chicago)); 212-217 (no photograph in eBL: IM.76854 (Iraq Museum)); 218b-220 (no photograph in eBL: IM.76854 (Iraq Museum)); 225-226 (no photograph in eBL: IM.76854 (Iraq Museum); photograph does not show these lines (visual check): BM.34964); 231 (no photograph in eBL: ISACM-A.3444 (Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, Chicago)); 243 (no photograph in eBL: IM.76854 (Iraq Museum)); 247-268 (no photograph in eBL: IM.76941 (Iraq Museum)); 269-272 (no photograph in eBL: IM.76941 (Iraq Museum), IM.76854 (Iraq Museum)); 281-285 (no photograph in eBL: IM.76854 (Iraq Museum)); 286 (no photograph in eBL: ISACM-A.3444 (Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, Chicago), IM.76854 (Iraq Museum)); 294 (no photograph in eBL: IM.76854 (Iraq Museum)); 297 (no photograph in eBL: ISACM-A.3444 (Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, Chicago), IM.76854 (Iraq Museum)); 300 (no photograph in eBL: BM.72719, ISACM-A.3444 (Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, Chicago), IM.76854 (Iraq Museum)); 301-302 (no photograph in eBL: ISACM-A.3444 (Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures, Chicago), IM.76854 (Iraq Museum)); 322 (no manuscript preserves it). A line is shown only on a photographed tablet that carries it as text. Commentaries and other texts that quote a line (letters, rituals, god lists) are not used as witnesses, because they carry it with explanations or inside another text; tablets without a photograph in eBL are not used, because the line could not be shown on its tablet.
translator_notes: Akkadian: eBL transliteration of the signs on the photographed tablet (manuscript-level ATF), not a composite text.
English: A. R. George's translation in the eBL edition; it renders eBL's composite text, including restorations from other tablets.
Line numbers: eBL edition (based on A. R. George, The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic, Oxford 2003). Each section also gives the tablet's own column and line numbers.

Signs in the Akkadian: [ ] broken away; x illegible sign; # damaged sign; ? uncertain reading; ! sign corrected by the editor; ... broken signs of unknown number; ( ) signs perhaps broken away; { } determinative; < > sign omitted by the scribe, supplied by the editor; / alternative readings; : divider sign written on the tablet; (line break) the line runs on to the next line of the tablet; (gloss: ...) a note written by the scribe in small signs or in the margin.

translation.original_ref: BM.38538 (George 2003 ms. o), reverse, column vi, line 16'b-17'a of the tablet = SB II 1
translation.scan_note: British Museum BM.38538: reverse, column vi, the tablet's own line 16'b-17'a. eBL's corpus edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/4/SB/II) attributes SB II 1 to this manuscript at these column and line numbers. Photograph checked: obverse, reverse and edges, ink number 38538 on the edge; one face carries about 15 lines running to the left edge, consistent with eBL's column vi (15 lines); the other face is worn. BM.38538, a copy of SB I, carries this line as its catch-line: the opening of the next tablet of the series, copied at the end of the previous one (eBL lists catch-lines among its quotations; unlike commentaries and quotations in other texts, a catch-line is the line itself on a copy of the work). On this tablet line 1 is partly broken (square brackets and x in the Akkadian). The English of this line translates eBL's composite text, so it includes words that are not preserved on this tablet but are restored from other manuscripts or by the editors. Square brackets in the English mark eBL's restorations in its composite text; words that survive on other tablets carry no brackets even where this tablet is broken.
